content:
Apple is opposing the Department of Justice's attempt to overturn a court decision that allows Apple to request documents from over a dozen federal agencies. Here's the full story.

A little background

A few weeks ago, Apple won the right to request documents from 14 U.S. agencies as part of its defence in the antitrust case filed by the Department of Justice in March 2024.

They include the following agencies and departments:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple's argument is that, if it can prove the federal government chose its products because of their privacy features, that evidence could support its claim that the practices challenged by the DOJ have legitimate justifications, rather than being anticompetitive conduct.

After Apple won this dispute, the DOJ filed a motion asking retired federal judge Jose Linares—who is serving as the special master in the case—to reconsider his decision.

In complex cases involving large amounts of document discovery, courts sometimes appoint a special master to handle narrower disputes in order to ease the workload of the presiding judge. A special master can be a retired judge, a practising attorney, or another expert with relevant experience.

In its motion, the DOJ asked the court to overturn Apple's win on discovery, arguing that Judge Linares applied the wrong legal standard by treating the relevant agencies as parties to the case, rather than as non-parties entitled to greater protection in document discovery.

The DOJ also argued that Apple's demands would impose an unreasonable burden on the relevant agencies, citing 13 newly submitted affidavits as support, and noted that the documents have limited relevance because federal agencies are not "ordinary consumers".

"This motion is without merit in every respect"

Apple's response to the DOJ's motion has been made public, and the company did not hold back in refuting every one of the DOJ's arguments for overturning the decision.

Citing multiple precedents, Apple wrote that "the Special Master correctly applied the legal standard for discovery against federal agencies as parties," then proceeded to dismantle the DOJ's arguments on unreasonable burden and relevance one by one.

In its conclusion, Apple said:

Under the schedule set by Judge Linares on August 4, no further briefing will be accepted, and it is now up to him to decide whether to keep the original discovery order in place or grant the DOJ's request for reconsideration.
